structure.title: Expanding empires
structure.text: Early books trace rulers, peoples, customs, and the growth of Persian power through stories and competing reports.

structure.title: War and explanation
structure.text: Later books concentrate on the Persian invasions of Greece, while speeches and digressions continue to test why events happened.

people.name: Croesus
people.text: A wealthy king whose judgments matter early.

people.name: Inquiry
people.text: Herodotus' collection and assessment of accounts.

context.title: Reporting and believing
context.text: Herodotus sometimes records a story without endorsing it. His qualifications help distinguish testimony, hearsay, and personal judgment.
context.takeaway: Attend to how he says he knows.

context.title: Customs in comparison
context.text: Accounts of other peoples interrupt the military story because ways of living also explain political action and misunderstanding.
context.takeaway: A digression may supply an explanation.

notice.text: Track warnings that powerful people dismiss.
notice.why: Confidence can become a cause of disaster.

notice.text: Compare rival versions of an event.
notice.why: Historical explanation emerges through disagreement rather than one unbroken account.

opening: Croesus has wealth, power, and an oracle whose answer seems to promise victory. He goes to war and discovers that a prophecy can be perfectly accurate while meaning something other than he hoped. Herodotus collects such failures of understanding as he investigates how Greeks and Persians came to fight. Kings, travellers, priests, and rival witnesses supply his material. The result has the curiosity of someone who cannot pass a good story, and the seriousness of someone asking how entire peoples become enemies.
